scores.strengths: Cleanest compliance posture of the three. The Challenger Protocol is the single best governance object in any proposal: every adaptive rule lives in exactly one of three states (shadow/challenger/online), the frozen parameters are the permanent null hypothesis, promotion only on scheduled review dates with pre-registered win criteria (DSR of the difference, PBO, bootstrap CI) — this is the strongest structural defense of the frozen estimation standards. Stage-1 completeness, Stage-2 switchability (multiplier pinned to 1 when off), and Stage-3 equity-only scope are all respected verbatim and the 'What stays unchanged' section explicitly re-affirms each frozen item with reasons. Trial meter increments BEFORE results are viewed, including abandoned agent attempts and sweep cells — the tightest wording of the trial-count rule. Shadow GMM correctly gated behind non-trading status and 10+ observed transitions. Hedge grid correctly discovers the SEBI FutEq infeasibility at Conservative top-end in design.
scores.weaknesses: Rhetorical overreach smuggles untestable claims: 'the 2022 stock-bond correlation break is the PROOF the frozen parts are right' (a single episode is not proof), 'the AI-age sweep's own verdict', 'every credible firm's AI deployment pattern independently converged here' — unverifiable appeals to authority. E|f|=10/cap ±20 is imported as a convention without flagging that the cap value itself needs a grid justification; '6-12 month' probation windows are ranges, not grids. The quarterly Ilmanen dashboard 'informing haircut-Kelly numerators' is an under-specified channel — if human-mediated, it leaks judgment into Stage-1 sizing; the proposal never states whether this flows by rule or by discretion. Weakest of the three on the 2-person frozen constraint: no principal time budget, no explicit scope ceiling, no statement of what is ruthlessly NOT built — operational overload is itself a threat to the binding drawdown discipline. Archive 'size capped' with no mechanism for setting the cap.

scores.strengths: Contains the single most original compliance idea across all three: LLM-sourced hypotheses flagged at registration because pretraining contamination means the agent's PRIORS are lookahead, requiring post-cutoff/out-of-corpus validation windows — this extends the frozen 'LLM backtests inadmissible' rule to its logical conclusion and no other proposal has it. Only proposal to state actual pre-registered grids inline (IC grid {0.02, 0.05, 0.10}), which is exactly what 'grids and ranks only' demands. The feedback-loop table with a named guardrail per loop (FL1-FL10) is the most auditable statement of adaptivity anywhere. Fast/slow split thesis is coherent. Honest epistemics: 'some sleeves will become formally unknowable; that is the correct answer', 'validate the OI substitute before trusting it', 'validate India-specific bleed first'.
scores.weaknesses: Enforcement problems the other two avoid. (1) Scope smudge in Stage 3: 'skfolio rails for walk-forward/CombinatorialPurgedCV/STACKING inside the cross-section' — stacking is signal combination, i.e. return-engine estimation, not construction; sliding it into construct/ blurs the frozen Stage-3 boundary (equity cross-section optimization only). (2) The architecture diagram routes 'PolicyTargets' out of construct/ into overlay/ — as drawn, Stage 3 emits policy, which would violate 'asset mix is policy, never optimized'; the text contradicts the diagram, but a contract enforcer reads what is written. (3) 'Adaptivity-first' framing admits adaptivity through many parallel channels (rotation ledger, lifecycle, ensemble drift, decay engine, crowding) each individually guarded but with no unified promotion protocol like the Challenger Protocol — more surface area for drift over 14 years, and over-adaptation is the failure mode the proposal itself names as the dominant killer. (4) Same untestable rhetoric ('only appreciating asset', 'edge least arbitraged') and same under-specified Ilmanen-to-Kelly channel. (5) Weekly funnel triage plus 13 modules with no principal time accounting strains the 2-person constraint.

scores.strengths: Best fit to the two frozen constraints the other proposals treat as background: the 2-person team and the binding drawdown governor. Principal attention is budgeted explicitly (30min/day to 3 days/year), monitoring is inverted to exception-driven (one fixed-format RAG page — 'anything that doesn't fit on it doesn't get monitored'), and Section 8 ('Ruthlessly cut') is the only place any proposal states what will NOT be built — patterns not dependencies, SQLite not MLflow server, a new sleeve requires retiring one. Strongest structural enforcement of the estimation standards: kill-switch 7 makes any run reading outside the as-of API fail CI and be inadmissible as evidence — 'discipline in CI, not in virtue' is the operational form of the frozen standards. The data kill-switch (never trade unverified data, de-risk one rung) and the runbook with a complete kill-switch battery directly serve the binding drawdown constraint. Retro-registering death certificates for already-live sleeves (Q2 build order) closes a gap both other proposals leave open. PBO thresholds stated as a grid {0.1, 0.25, 0.5}. Division-of-labor section with both parties' TOPS believability scored is the most concrete governance for principal+Claude. Minimum-module-set (Section 10) shows which pieces carry the binding constraints if everything else stalls.
scores.weaknesses: Sprinkles the most raw numbers: max 11 modules, ≤5 triggers/≤6 actions, ≤3 survivors/week, one page, 90%-of-benefit claims, time budgets — defensible as governance scope caps rather than fitted parameters (the frozen no-magic-numbers rule is an estimation standard), but none carries a grid or a derivation, and a few ('two timestamp columns capture 90% of the benefit') are untestable claims stated as fact. VineCopula synthetic stress paths as the governor's 'test suite' flirts with synthetic evidence for the binding constraint and needs an explicit inadmissibility fence. Lacks a unified Challenger Protocol — adaptivity promotion is scattered across locks, certs, and the rotation ledger rather than one formal object with the frozen incumbent as permanent null. Same under-specified Ilmanen-to-Kelly-numerator channel as the others. Quarterly (not monthly) impact refit is asserted without justification against the sibling proposals' monthly cadence.

scores.strengths: The Challenger Protocol is the single best idea in the whole exercise: a clean three-state rule (shadow -> challenger vs frozen null -> online reduce-only, promotion only on scheduled review dates, frozen parameters as the permanent null hypothesis) that answers the hardest question — how adaptivity gets admitted at all — in one paragraph the desk can actually enforce. Migration order is correctly ranked by evidence integrity (recorder/trial meter first, perishable capture second). The 'walk-forward concatenation from registration date is the signal's only standing evidence' rule is the right death blow to re-run backtests. Statement of the trial meter (every abandoned agent attempt and every sweep cell counted before results are viewed) is the cleanest of the three. Crisis-insurance currency for the trend/hedge blocks directly serves the binding constraint.
scores.weaknesses: It is the least operational of the three: no principal attention budget, no daily runbook with clock times, no statement of what the human actually sees each day — the monitor plane lists daily CUSUM + crowding + TE + capture health + shadow logs with no aggregation surface, which is exactly the 'monitoring nobody reads' failure mode at a 2-person desk. Monthly impact refits on own-fill samples are optimistic even shrunk to prior — a desk this size gets a handful of meaningful builds per month. The governance section stacks quarterly Ilmanen + influence review + rotation review + half-life refit on top of monthly attribution with no time accounting; cadence honesty is asserted, not demonstrated. Module count (11 + governance + a separate three-state protocol) has no ceiling and no cut list — nothing is ever explicitly declared out of scope.

scores.strengths: The fast/slow split is the best organizing thesis of the three — it gives a principled answer for every future 'should this adapt?' question rather than case-by-case litigation. The feedback-loop table (FL1–FL10) with an explicit guardrail per loop is exactly the artifact a 2-person desk needs on the wall. Uniquely flags LLM hypothesis provenance: pretraining contamination means the agent's priors are themselves lookahead, so LLM-sourced ideas require post-cutoff/out-of-corpus validation windows — no other proposal catches this, and it matters more every year to 2040. Notes the 'formally unknowable is a valid answer' point on uniqueness weighting. Migration steps are each independently useful.
scores.weaknesses: It is adaptivity-first in name and in temperament: a weekly research cycle, quarterly rotation of online parameter sets, rolling refit task lists, and ten live feedback loops is more model churn than one principal can audit — the rotation ledger makes swapping models cheap, and cheap swapping is the disease the frozen rules exist to prevent. skfolio as an actual dependency (vs the pattern-only stance of the other two) adds 14-year maintenance risk for marginal benefit. Like anti-overfit, it has no daily surface — monitoring is enumerated by cadence but never aggregated into something a human reads in ten minutes. No scope ceiling, no cut list, no minimum viable set: when the build stalls (it will), nothing tells the desk what to protect. Lacks the Challenger Protocol's crisp promotion/demotion symmetry — adaptivity guardrails are per-loop rather than one uniform admission rule.

scores.strengths: The only proposal that would survive contact with a 2-person desk, because it is the only one that treats principal attention as the binding constraint and budgets it explicitly (30 min/day, 2h/week, half-day/month, 2 days/quarter, 3 days/year). The daily runbook with IST clock times, the one-page RAG-header sentinel (green = skip; push only on amber/red), the enumerated kill-switches (including the data kill-switch: trade on last-good snapshot AND de-risk a rung), the division-of-labor section, and the 'ruthlessly cut' list (patterns not dependencies, SQLite+parquet, no MLflow server, module ceiling of 11, a new sleeve requires retiring one, no meeting a rule can replace) are exactly what 'runbook clarity and honest cadences' means. Quarterly (not monthly) impact refits is the honest cadence for a desk whose own-fill sample is small. The 'minimum module set / the 90%' section is the only acknowledgment in any proposal that builds stall — it tells the desk what to protect when they do. Weekly triage capped at <=3 survivors converts the AI-throughput problem into a bounded human gate. Deferring chrono-LLM text signals and the flow sleeve to year 2 is honest sequencing, not omission. Contains substantially all of the technical content of the other two (bitemporal store, bias CI, CPCV/PBO, death certs, crowding, policy grammar, forecast currency/Grinold, xrisk+TE, netting, TOPS/meta-label, fills ledger).
scores.weaknesses: Lacks the Challenger Protocol's single uniform admission rule for adaptivity — its guardrails are scattered across the feedback-loop table rather than unified, which will invite case-by-case relitigating in year 6. 'Claude repairs fetchers same-day' and the 18:30->20:30 daily window are tight; a realistic runbook would state the degraded-mode path when EOD files land late (the data kill-switch partially covers this but isn't wired to the schedule). Misses the LLM-provenance/contamination flag on agent-sourced hypotheses. The both-parties-scored TOPS framing ('the principal's believability can fall') is a nice line but has no stated consequence, so it is decoration.

scores.strengths: The most rigorous epistemics of the three. The Challenger Protocol is the single best object in any proposal: a complete, symmetric, pre-registered state machine (shadow -> challenger vs frozen null -> online reduce-only, promotion only on scheduled review dates, frozen params as the null forever) that answers the decade's hardest question — how to admit adaptivity without capitulation — in one mechanism. Structural (not procedural) enforcement everywhere: bitemporal as-of API, trial meter that counts abandoned agent attempts and sweep cells BEFORE results are viewed, bias CI for code-level lookahead, 'the agent proposes, the harness disposes'. Crisis-insurance currency for the hedge grid, the never-let-benign-months-loosen-participation-caps clause, and the regulatory-break registry allowed to answer 'insufficient post-break data' are exactly the details a 2035 retrospective vindicates. Migration order (harness first, capture second) is correct.
scores.weaknesses: From 2035: the likeliest failure is not statistical but operational, and this proposal never budgets the desk's scarcest resource. No principal-attention accounting, no single monitoring surface, no scope ceiling, no minimum-viable fallback if the build stalls or AI tooling underdelivers — eleven heavyweight modules plus a five-tier funnel plus three ritual cadences for two people is a plan that gets 60% built and then rots, and a half-built enforcement harness is worse than a checklist because it confers false confidence. Second-order risk: the Challenger Protocol's long promotion windows plus 6-12 month paper probation mean that if decay ran FASTER than 2026 consensus, validated signals arrive at the book already half-dead; the proposal prices Type-I error superbly and Type-II error not at all. No kill-switches for data/capture failure or execution anomaly.

scores.strengths: The fast/slow split is the clearest articulation of the correct design thesis (fast where data is abundant and feedback quick; slow where samples are scarce and pain is the tempter), and every adaptive element names its guardrail — the feedback-loop table with cadence + guard per loop is the best single page in any proposal and directly auditable in 2035. Unique and genuinely important: flagging hypothesis provenance so LLM-sourced ideas require post-cutoff/out-of-corpus validation windows, because pretraining contamination makes the agent's PRIORS a form of lookahead — none of the other proposals catch this, and by 2030 most hypotheses will be LLM-sourced. Rotation ledger elevated correctly ('when do we swap the model' drives more P&L than the models). skfolio rails over bespoke code is the right 2-person call.
scores.weaknesses: From 2035: largely the same architecture as anti-overfit with a riskier flag on it. 'Adaptivity-first' as the organizing principle is the wrong sign for the historically dominant killer (over-adaptation), and while each loop has a guardrail, the proposal lacks the one mechanism that makes adaptivity safe as a CLASS — anti-overfit's challenger-vs-frozen-null protocol; here promotion paths are per-mechanism and less uniform, which over 14 years is where drift gets in. Same operational blindness as anti-overfit: no attention budget, no daily surface, no scope caps, no degradation plan — plus MORE moving parts (10 feedback loops, weekly triage, quarterly rotation) for the same two people. If AI tools turned out WORSE than expected, this design has the most orphaned machinery.

scores.strengths: The only proposal that identifies and prices the true binding constraint: two people, ~30 min/day of principal attention, 14 years. It contains essentially all of the other two proposals' statistical machinery (harness/recorder-as-ledger, bias CI, CPCV/PBO, bitemporal store, break registry, death certs, crowding, ensemble-median R, policy grammar, FutEq-constrained hedge grid, TOPS/meta-label, fills ledger, TC-by-constraint, anti-capitulation lock, AGS, breadth budget) and then adds what they miss: the one-page RAG daily surface with pre-registered exception menus; an explicit kill-switch inventory (data kill = trade last-good AND de-risk a rung; execution kill; harness-integrity CI where any run reading outside the as-of API is inadmissible by construction); ruthless scope caps (11-module ceiling, new sleeve requires retiring one, <=3 typed objects, SQLite+parquet, patterns-not-dependencies); a quarter-by-quarter build order where each step ships value alone; and Section 10's minimum module set — the explicit graceful-degradation core that keeps the desk alive if the build stalls or AI tooling disappoints. That last section is precisely what the 2035 retrospective grades: resilience to the decade being different. Both parties' TOPS scores can fall, including the principal's — the only proposal that scores the human symmetrically.
scores.weaknesses: From 2035: the scope caps that save it can also ossify it — a hard 11-module ceiling and one-in-one-out sleeve rule could have blocked a genuinely new edge class mid-decade (caps are annually amendable, but the anti-capitulation culture will resist). Quarterly (vs monthly) impact refit is defensible but slower to catch a microstructure break. Its adaptivity admission path is the weakest of the three — it has the rotation ledger and reduce-only throttles but lacks anti-overfit's uniform Challenger Protocol, so each adaptive mechanism's promotion rules are bespoke; over 14 years that heterogeneity is a drift surface. Misses ai-adaptive's LLM-provenance/contaminated-priors flag entirely. The daily-page 'green = skip' convention risks trained inattention before the one red day that matters.

must_keep: The Challenger Protocol (anti-overfit): every adaptive rule lives in exactly one of {shadow, challenger, online}; challengers paper-trade against the frozen incumbent with pre-registered win criteria (DSR of the difference, PBO, bootstrap CI excluding zero); promotion/demotion symmetric, rule-driven, only on scheduled review dates; frozen parameters are the null hypothesis forever. Graft this onto the winner as the uniform adaptivity-admission law.

R as the median of an ensemble of pre-registered grid variants of the unchanged ladder; first response to detected drift is uncertainty-widening/de-risking via existing buckets, never refitting; shadow GMM logged non-trading with disagreements feeding the research queue (all three).
